title: My house, my father
goal: Use possessives with the letter changes they bring, and talk about feelings and aches with the preposition *ar*.
bekal: put *mo, do, a, ár, bhur, a* in front of nouns with the right séimhiú or urú

notes: **Mo theach, do thae — possessives bring séimhiú.** *Mo* ("my") and *do* ("your") always soften the next letter: *teach* → *mo theach*, *tae* → *do thae*, *carr* → *mo charr*, *mála* → *mo mhála*. If the noun starts with a vowel, the possessive shrinks: *mo athair* becomes **m'athair**, *do aghaidh* becomes **d'aghaidh** — like English "I'm". The same happens before *f*: séimhiú makes *f* silent, so *mo fón* becomes **m'fhón** and *do fear* becomes **d'fhear**.

**Tá tinneas cinn orm — even pain sits on top of you.** Irish doesn't say "I have a headache" but "there's a headache on me". You saw this pattern in Unit 2 with *ocras* (hunger), and now it's complete: nearly all feelings and physical complaints use *ar*, while *tá … agam* (Unit 7) is for possessions. *Tá slaghdán orm*, not *agam*.

**Tá mo scornach tinn — body parts use the possessive.** When you name the body part itself, Irish goes back to the ordinary pattern: *Tá mo scornach tinn* ("my throat is sore"), *Tá mo chos tinn* ("my leg hurts"). The short rule: **feelings** take *ar*, **body parts** take a possessive.

**Ná bí buartha — saying "don't".** Commands use the base form of the verb (*fan* = stay, *ól* = drink). To say "don't", put *ná* in front: *Ná bí buartha* ("don't worry"), *Ná téigh* ("don't go"), *Ná déan sin* ("don't do that"). *Ná* causes no letter change.

blocks.text: Six possessives, three patterns of change. Read this table alongside the séimhiú and urú tables in the pronunciation chapter — this is where those two rules are used most.

blocks.title: Three a's spelled exactly alike
items: All three are written with the same *a* and pronounced the same short vowel. The only thing that tells them apart is the change to the next word. This is the strongest reason séimhiú and urú can't be ignored: here they aren't decoration, they carry the meaning.

sections.title: Ar — feelings that sit on top of you

blocks.text: Watch out for *uirthi* ("on her") — it strays far from the others and is said "IR-hih". It's the only one you need to learn separately.

blocks.title: Tá brón orm — the most useful apology
items: Literally "there's sorrow on me", and it's used just like "I'm sorry" — for regret, not for "excuse me".
For **excuse me** — interrupting someone, passing in front of them, getting attention — use *Gabh mo leithscéal* ("take my excuse").
To offer condolences: *Ba mhaith liom comhbhrón a dhéanamh leat* — or, far more often, *Tá brón orm faoi do chailliúint* ("sorry for your loss").

sections.title: An corp — the body, and saying you feel unwell

blocks.title: Teanga — one word, two meanings
items: *Teanga* means both **tongue** and **language**, just like English "mother tongue" or Latin *lingua*.
*An Ghaeilge — ár dteanga féin* means "Irish — our own language", a line you'll often see on posters and school signs.
Notice *ár dteanga*: the possessive "our" brings urú, so the *t* is covered by a *d*. The word is said with a d sound — "awr DYAN-guh".
